To preserve the passive membrane physics, we use the inverse cylinder transformation to construct a positively regressive coefficient $p_m$. The resulting delta-dynamic equation is exactly the restriction to $\mathbb{T}$ of the classical continuous-time LIF trajectory. detail.abstract_excerpt: The game "Mafia'' is a social deduction game where $n$ players attempt to uncover a covert coalition of $m$ players among the $n$. Typically, $d=1$ of the non-coalition players are labelled ``Detective'' and have special abilities. Most game-theoretic analysis considers, however, only the variant without a Detective. Once the Detective role is introduced, extremely complex strategies can be employed, for which reason only upper and lower bounds for winning have been established, namely by considering specific strategies. We analyse the case $m=d=1$, providing a first example where an explicit, provably-optimal strategy can be described beyond $d=0$.

[...] Window management, metacity, workspaces, tiling, XWayland, clipboard and clipman support, multiple monitors, display scaling, hotplugging, screenshots, screen sharing, and session management are all working. I've also added desktop effects: fade, zoom, zap, spin, squeemize, magic lamp, desktop cube, expo, and wobbly windows.

items.headline: Infrastructure for Verifiable AI: Where Proof Costs Go and How Hardware Can Help
items.summary: Users of artificial intelligence services, including those powered by large language models and other transformer-based models, need assurance that inference and training follow the declared computation without exposing private models or data. Zero-knowledge proofs can provide this assurance, but proof generation remains expensive. Hardware acceleration research often reports gains for individual cryptographic operations, leaving their effect on the full cost of proving neural-network workloads, particularly large transformer models, unclear.

detail.problem_context: Users of artificial intelligence services, including those powered by large language models and other transformer-based models, need assurance that inference and training follow the declared computation without exposing private models or data.
detail.method_architecture: Zero-knowledge proofs can provide this assurance, but proof generation remains expensive. Hardware acceleration research often reports gains for individual cryptographic operations, leaving their effect on the full cost of proving neural-network workloads, particularly large transformer models, unclear.
detail.findings_tradeoffs: We introduce a four-layer framework linking verifiable AI workloads, proof systems, cryptographic kernels and hardware platforms, use it to review the literature, and add original measurements of six provers and seven kernels to identify which costs matter in practice. Our measurements show that the dominant cost changes with the proof system and input length. In low-rank fine-tuning, the cost of opening commitments to fixed model weights remains nearly constant across input lengths from 64 to 2048, while the work associated with intermediate values grows. A 13-billion-parameter fine-tuning configuration exceeds the capacity of a 40-gigabyte graphics processor but completes on an 80-gigabyte device, showing why capacity must be assessed alongside execution time. Our kernel profiling further identifies instruction issue and synchronization limits that a bandwidth-only model misses. We use these findings to assess graphics processors, reconfigurable logic, custom chips and existing artificial intelligence accelerators. The resulting research agenda connects proof-friendly numeric formats, reuse of fixed-weight commitments, heterogeneous execution and shared benchmarks to the measured bottlenecks. Effective acceleration requires selecting hardware and proof-system optimizations around the cost profile of the target workload.

detail.abstract_excerpt: Users of artificial intelligence services, including those powered by large language models and other transformer-based models, need assurance that inference and training follow the declared computation without exposing private models or data. Zero-knowledge proofs can provide this assurance, but proof generation remains expensive. Hardware acceleration research often reports gains for individual cryptographic operations, leaving their effect on the full cost of proving neural-network workloads, particularly large transformer models, unclear. We introduce a four-layer framework linking verifiable AI workloads, proof systems, cryptographic kernels and hardware platforms, use it to review the literature, and add original measurements of six provers and seven kernels to identify which costs matter in practice. Our measurements show that the dominant cost changes with the proof system and input length. In low-rank fine-tuning, the cost of opening commitments to fixed model weights remains nearly constant across input lengths from 64 to 2048, while the work associated with intermediate values grows. A 13-billion-parameter fine-tuning configuration exceeds the capacity of a 40-gigabyte graphics processor but completes on an 80-gigabyte device, showing why capacity must be assessed alongside execution time. Our kernel profiling further identifies instruction issue and synchronization limits that a bandwidth-only model misses. We use these findings to assess graphics processors, reconfigurable logic, custom chips and existing artificial intelligence accelerators. The resulting research agenda connects proof-friendly numeric formats, reuse of fixed-weight commitments, heterogeneous execution and shared benchmarks to the measured bottlenecks. Effective acceleration requires selecting hardware and proof-system optimizations around the cost profile of the target workload.

items.headline: What Does It Cost to Force-Close a Lightning Channel? Evidence from 974,000 Channel Closes, 2018-2026
items.summary: Bitcoin's Lightning payment network returns the funds of a channel that cannot close cooperatively through pre-signed transactions whose fees and delays fall on its operators. That fee design is being replaced: Bitcoin Core 31.0 removed the mempool rule anchor channels relied on, and the Lightning specification adopted zero-fee commitments in May 2026. What the old design costs has never been measured across fee regimes.

detail.problem_context: Bitcoin's Lightning payment network returns the funds of a channel that cannot close cooperatively through pre-signed transactions whose fees and delays fall on its operators.
detail.method_architecture: That fee design is being replaced: Bitcoin Core 31.0 removed the mempool rule anchor channels relied on, and the Lightning specification adopted zero-fee commitments in May 2026. What the old design costs has never been measured across fee regimes.
detail.findings_tradeoffs: We trace every public channel close and every force close on-chain from January 2018 to October 2026, 973,581 closes, and follow each output to its spend. A separate chain index confirms all 698,476 public closes we could compare. Fee spikes did not bring a wave of force closes. Force closes in a spike week and the next were 0.97 times the four weeks before, against 1.02 after ordinary weeks of the same years. A force close costs 2-6 times a cooperative close in fees and locks the closer's balance for days, which outweighs the fees only in low-fee years. When fees are high, pending payments are exposed: in 2023, 18.2% of HTLC timeouts confirmed more than 40 blocks after expiry. Yet since 2021, forwarding nodes lost only 38 payments, each with the preimage already on-chain. Anchor outputs cut late timeouts in fee spikes (20.6% against 30.5%), yet owners rarely bump commitments with them, and miners take most of what third parties sweep. Zero-fee commitments would save only 12% of the anchor mechanism's block space; they should be judged by how promptly payments resolve when fees spike.

detail.method_architecture: Current state-of-the-art protein language models (PLMs) primarily scale parameter size on sequence corpora to capture evolutionary constraints but remain blind to the explicit physical dynamics of folded proteins. Conversely, models trained strictly on physical dynamics neglect critical evolutionary sequence statistics.
detail.findings_tradeoffs: In this paper, we bridge this gap by introducing DynamicsPLM, a highly parameter-efficient 35-million-parameter model that unifies evolutionary and biophysical representation learning. Utilizing a second-stage, multi-task continual pretraining strategy on over 60,000 proteins, we enrich a foundational sequence encoder with explicit residue-level and pairwise molecular dynamics heads while preserving its original evolutionary knowledge. At inference, DynamicsPLM computes zero-shot mutation effects from sequence alone by balancing an evolutionary plausibility score against a structural dynamics disruption score. Across the massive ProteinGym benchmark and natural variants of the Tsuboyama folding stability dataset, DynamicsPLM achieves state-of-the-art accuracy among all models under 100M parameters, and matches or outperforms several billion-scale sequence-based models of its size. Our findings demonstrate that explicit structural-dynamics supervision provides a parameter-efficient alternative to raw scale. Availability: All codes including data preparation scripts, training and validation recipes, and experimental configurations for LoMuS are available at: https://github.com/kabir-ai2bio-lab/DynamicsPLM.

detail.problem_context: RNA foundation models with diverse architectures have shown promise for learning representations of messenger RNA (mRNA) sequences.
detail.method_architecture: However, existing benchmarks commonly reduce token-level embeddings to transcript-level representations through global mean pooling before fitting a downstream probe. This aggregation does not explicitly preserve the identities of biologically distinct mRNA regions.
detail.findings_tradeoffs: Consequently, signals associated with short regulatory regions may be diluted, confounding assessments of representation quality with the information preserved by the readout. We introduce an architecture-agnostic, region-aware readout that separately averages embeddings within the 5$'$ untranslated region (UTR), coding sequence, and 3$'$ UTR and concatenates the resulting representations for linear probing. We reproduce mRNABench evaluations for 20 frozen models from 18 families, with a median absolute score difference of 0.0009 across 380 model--dataset--target evaluations published for 19 models, and construct a region-aware benchmark using the same models, tasks, and splits. Relative to global mean pooling, region-aware pooling increases Pearson correlation, averaged across the 20 models, by 11--25% on translation and stability tasks, with no statistically significant decreases detected for any model on the regression tasks. On classification tasks, relative changes in the area under the precision--recall curve range from $-3%$ to $+11%$. Boundary randomization and displacement generally reduce performance, while dimensionality-matched and sequence-composition controls indicate that the gains are not explained solely by increased feature dimensionality, region length, or guanine--cytosine (GC) content. Learned attention pooling approaches region-aware performance only when supplied with one query per region. In silico perturbations reveal stronger sensitivity to upstream AUGs (uAUGs) and their Kozak context, while analyses of endogenous transcripts show approximately threefold greater recovery of length- and GC-adjusted uAUG-associated differences than global-mean probes. Both readouts capture codon optimality. Model rankings averaged over the regression tasks remain largely stable, while within a task models move by several places. Our region-aware benchmark therefore provides a biologically structured and complementary evaluation of mRNA foundation models, revealing regulatory information that is less accessible to linear probes after global mean pooling. items.headline: deepTools4: Faster, Scalable, and Modernized Genomic Data Analysis. The deepTools suite is widely used for quality control, summarization, and visualization of high-throughput sequencing data.
items.summary: The deepTools suite is widely used for quality control, summarization, and visualization of high-throughput sequencing data. items.headline: Bait: Mitigating Harmful Agentic Reinforcement Learning via Probing Reward Function
items.summary: We expose a safety vulnerability on nascent agentic reinforcement-learning-as-a-service. Specifically, with a cost as low as $20, we show that safety alignment of a large language model (e.g., Inkling) can be completely subverted through rounds of harmful agentic reinforcement learning (agentic RL) with a toxic environment from its users. We also demonstrate that upon a successful harmful agentic RL attack via the service API, the attackers can potentially use the safety-degraded model to assist with real-world harmful activities, e.g., exploit software vulnerabilities and launch code re-use attacks.

items.headline: Snoopie: A Multi-GPU Communication Profiler and Visualizer
items.summary: With data movement becoming one of the most expensive bottlenecks in computing, the need for profiling tools to analyze communication becomes crucial for effectively scaling multi-GPU applications. While existing profiling tools including first-party software by GPU vendors are robust and excel at capturing compute operations within a single GPU, support for monitoring GPU-GPU data transfers and calls issued by communication libraries is currently inadequate. To fill these gaps, we introduce Snoopie, an instrumentation-based multi-GPU communication profiling tool built on NVBit, capable of tracking peer-to-peer transfers and GPU-centric communication library calls.

items.headline: Package managers have an integrity problem
items.summary: I tested 25 of the most popular package managers to check whether they detect a compromised package repository injecting malicious code into legitimate packages. This code integrity problem could be solved using cryptographic hashes or signatures, but many package managers are still vulnerable to this threat. Of the 25 package managers reviewed 1 , fewer than half used lockfiles that checked for tampering by default, and only two verified the integrity of every package they downloaded.

detail.problem_context: I tested 25 of the most popular package managers to check whether they detect a compromised package repository injecting malicious code into legitimate packages.
detail.method_architecture: This code integrity problem could be solved using cryptographic hashes or signatures, but many package managers are still vulnerable to this threat. Of the 25 package managers reviewed 1 , fewer than half used lockfiles that checked for tampering by default, and only two verified the integrity of every package they downloaded.
detail.findings_tradeoffs: Supply-chain attacks caused by developer compromise are a common story, but imagine what happens if ongoing mitigation attempts, including work by Trail of Bits 2 , are successful. If developers of popular packages are no longer the easiest targets, attackers will shift their focus to the next weakest link in the system: the package repositories that serve the code. The cryptographic answers to this problem are more subtle than they appear, and many implementations fall short due to deliberate design choices, resource prioritization, or the complexity of developer-friendly solutions. One natural answer is to include a cryptographic hash of a package’s contents in a lockfile and compare hashes after downloading the package. This automatic verification was the default behavior in about half of the package managers I tested, but others required extra configuration to include or verify these hashes, used hashes in a cryptographically insecure way, or lacked hashes entirely. This is summarized in the following table. Verifies integrity Go, vcpkg Verifies if lockfile is present Bun, Bundler, Cargo, npm, pnpm, Poetry, SwiftPM, uv, Yarn Verifies with lockfile + extra steps Conda, Gradle, Pip, NuGet, Pub Does not verify with lockfile or N/A CocoaPods, Composer, Conan, cpanminus, Gem, Maven, PowerShellGet, PSResourceGet, R Table 1: Lockfile-based security of a package manager fetching dependencies from a malicious repository, categorized by how much work it takes a developer to achieve integrity. Experimentally verified for a particular configuration. Caveats detailed below. Another natural approach is to use signatures, avoiding the need to securely distribute a hash for every package. However, in my tests, only Go verified signatures by default; others required extra configuration, lacked verification code, or did not support signatures. Verifies signatures Go Verifies with configuration Bundler, Gem, Gradle, Maven, npm, NuGet Missing or incomplete verification Bun, cpanminus, Pip, pnpm, Poetry, PowerShellGet, PSResourceGet, uv, Yarn No signatures available for verification Cargo, CocoaPods, Composer, Conan, Conda, Pub, R, SwiftPM, vcpkg Table 2: Signature-based security of various package managers. Also experimentally verified and subject to similar caveats. As both tables show, I found a surprising variation in the cryptographic designs and the level of protection they provide. Despite the challenges, I also found several communities on the frontier of this integrity problem that are bringing improved designs to reality. This post explores those variations, showing where certain designs fall short, why code integrity is harder to solve than it appears, and what cryptographic designs might be adopted in the future. Simulating malicious package repositories Studying the cryptographic behavior of 25 package managers is quite the challenge. I wanted to minimize manual analysis, but also be 100% confident when I claim an attack from a malicious package repository is possible. To solve this problem, I built a testing harness based on Docker containers and mitmproxy that dynamically evaluates the security of package managers against a malicious server. Figure 1: Experimental design of the test harness used to simulate malicious package repositories The Ubuntu-based Docker images include a package manager, sample code, and optionally a lockfile. There are conflicting opinions about whether to include lockfiles in source code repositories, so I tested both configurations. The harness instructs the package manager to fetch dependencies from the repository, and the resulting network request routes through a WireGuard network to a custom mitmproxy addon. Because the mitmproxy TLS CA is installed in the Docker image, the addon can fully manipulate the plaintext from the package repository, simulating a compromised server. I assumed any web-facing server could be compromised (e.g., Composer fetches metadata from Packagist and packages from GitHub), but backend resources, like any private signing keys, remain secure. The simulated repository embeds malicious code into the downloaded packages, and if the sample code executes the malware, the attack is successful. I tried to keep the experimental setup reflective of real-world usage, but there are limitations. I installed the latest package manager versions, followed quickstart guides for setting up sample projects inside the container, and picked popular packages from public repositories to infect. I ran package manager commands with default flags to see if extra steps, like modifying the project manifest or running extra commands, were needed to enforce cryptographic integrity. However, I am limited to testing a single package with a single package manager version on a single platform, and the test conditions (e.g., PowerShell and CocoaPods on Ubuntu) may not represent the most common usage patterns. The setup isn’t meant to show that every developer is vulnerable to a malicious package repository, just that a developer following reasonable conventions is. With the package managers installed and network intercept functional, one (mostly) promising observation is clear. HTTPS is (almost) everywhere Our harness architecture captures all network traffic, so it’s easy to test that package managers are using TLS and validating the certificates. In almost every package manager, they are. The exception is cpanminus, the frequently recommended package manager for Perl. cpanminus uses unencrypted HTTP by default to connect to the Perl package repository, allowing any active network attacker to inject malicious code into downloaded packages. This vulnerability has been known for years, but the cpanminus developer has not switched to HTTPS, since doing so would be a breaking change to default behavior. 3 Hash functions don’t always provide integrity By using the mitmproxy addon to modify the package repository responses, I could investigate how different package managers use cryptographic hashes. Hashes are a natural way to ensure that a downloaded file has not been tampered with, but the main question is how the package manager learns the correct hash in the first place. Microsoft’s vcpkg package manager for C and C++ libraries offers an interesting example. The package manager source code includes content hashes for thousands of dependencies. When a developer updates their library and wants to register the new content in vcpkg, they recompute the hash of their package and open a pull request against the vcpkg source code with the new hash and link to the package. When a package is downloaded by vcpkg, the hash is checked. So as long as the package manager is trusted, this approach is fully secure against a malicious package repository. 4 Hashes in lockfiles It is significantly more common that the package manager learns the correct hash via a lockfile. A lockfile is frequently created by a package manager, resides alongside a project’s source code, and references specific versions of dependencies needed by the project. If a developer checks a lockfile with cryptographic hashes into the source code repository, and the user’s package manager validates downloaded packages against the hashes, then the user’s dependencies perfectly match the developer’s. This is how it works for the Bun package manager for JavaScript projects. Installing a package with bun add updates the bun.lock lockfile; committing the lockfile to Git and calling bun install on another copy of the repo verifies the hash in the lockfile against the new copy of the dependency. Similar behavior is found in npm, pnpm, and Yarn (also JavaScript package managers); uv and Poetry (Python package managers); Bundler (for Ruby); Cargo (for Rust); and SwiftPM (for Swift). Other package managers support lockfiles, but with more steps than the standard add/restore process. Python’s Pip has experimental support for the pylock.toml format, and Conda has the optional library Conda lock . NuGet, the .NET package manager, generates a lockfile after adding the RestorePackagesWithLockFile property to the project. Many package managers (Maven, R, PowerShellGet, PSResourceGet, and cpanminus) do not have dedicated lockfiles, and some have lockfiles (Gradle’s gradle.lockfile 5 and Gem’s Gemfile.lock ) without hashes in them. Hashes present, but not for integrity Surprisingly, I found a few examples where the lockfiles had a hash, but could still be compromised by a malicious server. This is not necessarily reflective of a vulnerability, since the underlying behavior is clearly documented, but it shows how there are multiple valid opinions about how lockfiles should be structured and consumed. Nevertheless, a user who is accustomed to the behavior of one package manager may be surprised by that of another. The first example is the Pub package manager for Dart and Flutter. The following excerpt of a pubspec.lock file includes a SHA-256 hash for the uuid package. uuid : dependency : "direct main" description : name : uuid sha256 : "9b129329f58692f6e6578329498a8fe9fbe98f090beb764ffbb8ee2eadd01dcd" url : "https://pub.dev" source : hosted version : "4.6.0" If a user calls flutter pub get to fetch dependencies, Pub downloads the package from the pub.dev server and computes the hash of the returned binary. If there is a mismatch, Pub detects the error, but installs the package anyway. The existing content-hash from pubspec.lock doesn't match contents for: * uuid-4.6.0 from "https://pub.dev" This indicates one of: * The content has changed on the server since you created the pubspec.lock. * The pubspec.lock has been corrupted. The content-hashes in pubspec.lock has been updated. This is documented behavior , and requires the non-default --enforce-lockfile option to block installation 6 . Overwriting the lockfile after a hash mismatch was also the default behavior in pnpm until version 11.4 from May 2026, when it was changed to close “supply-chain holes.” Like Pub, pnpm also supported a non-default --frozen-lockfile flag, indicating that the previous behavior which updated the lockfile was expected. Next, here is an excerpt of a conan.lock file, used by the Conan package manager for C and C++. "requires" : [ "zlib/1.3.1#cac0f6daea041b0ccf42934163defb20%1765284699.337" ] , This includes the package name ( zlib ), the version number ( 1.3.1 ), a recipe revision cac0f6daea041b0ccf42934163defb20 , and a timestamp. The 128-bit revision is an MD5 hash that includes source code. However, this hash is not intended to provide cryptographic security, but rather serves as a unique identifier. When Conan installs dependencies using this lockfile, it uses the recipe revision hash to download a particular file from the ConanCenter repository, but it does not recompute the recipe hash. Even if it did, there’s a separate package revision hash for platform-specific binaries that is not in the lockfile, and MD5 collisions could allow an attacker to create two distinct recipes with different behavior but the same hash. The CocoaPods dependency manager for Swift and Objective-C has a similar pattern. Here is part of a Podfile.lock file for a project that uses the popular Files dependency. SPEC CHECKSUMS : Files : d88e31b84d65e754935053b1c584ea8e2320698a This 160-bit checksum is the SHA-1 hash of the Files Podspec , which contains the following link to the source code. CocoaPods uses this link to fetch the Git repository. "source" : { "git" : "https://github.com/johnsundell/files.git" , "tag" : "4.0.2" } , So even though the lockfile can prevent tampering with the GitHub URL in the Podspec (setting aside expensive SHA-1 collision attacks), a compromised GitHub server could just serve a malicious version of the repository with the same tag. Finally, the Composer dependency manager for PHP includes commit hashes in the composer.lock file, as in the following excerpt. "dist" : { "type" : "zip" , "url" : "https://api.github.com/repos/guzzle/psr7/zipball/b094ded77ee97a6027ad6cf0e8c7b9f88381814c" , "reference" : "b094ded77ee97a6027ad6cf0e8c7b9f88381814c" , "shasum" : "" } , However, even though the b094ded... commit hash uniquely identifies the code, the ZIP archive in the URL does not include the Git tree as a way to verify the hash. Once again, GitHub could serve a malicious ZIP archive without detection by Composer. Lockfiles have many roles besides supply-chain integrity The previous experimental results show that lockfile hashes often can be used to enforce package integrity, but this is not their sole or even original purpose. Alternatively, they can lock dependencies to a particular functionality, enable an easy way for application developers to share a consistent environment, or facilitate reproducible builds. Analyzing package manager lockfiles through the lens of supply-chain security is a recent interpretation that can be at odds with their original design. The recent change to pnpm’s --frozen-lockfile is one example. Another example of this tension is the question of whether the lockfile should be committed to version control. Most modern guidance recommends committing the lockfile for applications, since the final build environment is fully controlled. The question is more complicated for libraries, since package managers often ignore libraries’ lockfiles to avoid locking to conflicting transitive dependencies. Committing the lockfile makes it easier to develop the library by sharing a consistent build environment with other developers, but excluding the lockfile makes it easier to catch conflicts with different dependency versions before they are found by users. Many package managers recommend committing the lockfile for libraries (e.g., npm , pnpm , Poetry , uv , and Yarn ), some recommend excluding it (e.g., Bundler ), and some leave it up to the developer (e.g., Cargo ). Many of these questions are explored in a recent study by Gamage et al. The authors explore lockfile design decisions for seven package managers, analyze published projects, and perform semi-structured interviews with 15 developers. They find that the practice of committing a lockfile varies by which package manager is used, and categorize five benefits to using lockfiles, as perceived by the interview subjects: build determinism, integrity, transparency into indirect dependencies, debugging, and security scanning. Some of the developers also preferred to not use lockfiles, citing a preference for end users to resolve to the latest version of a dependency, which may have more bug fixes and vulnerability patches. The diversity of package manager designs and views surrounding the purpose of lockfiles makes it difficult to prescribe a single recommendation. With regard to supply-chain integrity, it is common, but not universal, to view lockfiles as a source of integrity that should be committed with the source code. For package managers with lockfiles that do not provide cryptographic integrity, it is worth considering whether their users share that expectation. Even when lockfile hashes can provide cryptographic integrity, locking to specific package hashes means that users do not immediately receive subsequent updates or security fixes, since the newer package has a different hash. This leads to frequent lockfile bumping to distribute the latest hashes. Wanting immediate updates is a separate concern from wanting package integrity, but the current, common approach of using hashes in lockfiles is at odds with that goal. In conclusion, lockfile hashes are often, but not always, effective at providing cryptographic integrity, but do not work in every situation. Signatures are common; verification is not Signatures are a natural way to address these shortcomings, but implementations frequently fall short. In theory, developers could sign every release with their own private key, and the package manager could check the signature of the package it downloads from the package repository. In fact, signatures are relatively common in different package ecosystems, but proper signature validation is surprisingly lacking. The reality of using signatures to provide code integrity is more nuanced than it seems, and package managers have different approaches to the problem. Many package managers have no signatures available. Arguably, vcpkg does not need them, because all package hashes are distributed with the manager, but this leaves Cargo, CocoaPods, Composer, Conan, Conda, Pub, R, and SwiftPM 7 . The Conan developers are aware and previously decided not to fix it, citing several implementation challenges and suggesting organizations where integrity is critical could run their own repository server. Cargo developers are actively considering different signing designs, but this effort is still in progress. Composer developers have been implementing many new protections against supply-chain attacks, with future plans for artifact integrity. Repository signing One straightforward approach, known as repository signing, is when the package repository signs every package once it’s uploaded, and the repository’s public key is distributed with the package manager. This doesn’t solve the problem of a totally compromised package repository, since a malicious package repository could legitimately sign a malicious package, but it would protect against untrusted mirrors or a partial compromise of a package repository’s serving infrastructure. Repository signatures are used by the npm Registry , the NuGet Registry , and the PAUSE server for Perl module distribution. In the npm Registry, signatures are distributed within package metadata with repository-specific public keys . NuGet Registry repository signatures are found in .signature.p7s files within the distributed ZIP package, again with repository-specific public keys . The PAUSE server takes a different approach, using its GPG key to batch sign the cryptographic hashes of several packages at a time. Developer signing Developer signing involves the developer maintaining the private key and signing the package before uploading it to the repository for distribution. This prevents the package repository from tampering with the contents, but it also provides a way for the package repository to authenticate the uploader. There are two common approaches for a developer asserting their public key. In the first approach, the public key is distributed out-of-band. The Maven Central repository (used by Maven and Gradle) and the RubyGems repository (used by the gem and Bundler package managers) both support this type of developer signing. Maven Central uses PGP signatures, and developer keys are distributed by public keyservers . RubyGems uses self-signed certificates, and their distribution is left to the developers (e.g., rspec ). The major difference is that developer signing is mandatory for Maven Central, and optional for RubyGems. Developer signing is rare for RubyGems, due to the lack of an established chain of trust, and a previous attempt to introduce a certificate authority failed . The second approach involves a chain of trust. The NuGet Registry and PowerShell Gallery both support developer signatures. Neither makes signatures mandatory, but the PowerShell Gallery recommends it and the NuGet Registry has strict requirements if developer signing is used. In both, the developer’s key must chain to a trusted CA , and acquiring a valid code-signing certificate can cost hundreds of dollars per year. The benefit of this approach is that trusted root certificates can be preinstalled on the platform, allowing package managers to verify public keys. One downside of developer signing is that developers are responsible for key management, and they can lose the ability to update their code if they lose access to their key. Identity-based signing An increasingly common middle ground is “identity-based” or “keyless” signing from Sigstore . Rather than require developers to manage long-term private keys, a developer can use Sigstore’s Fulcio CA to issue a fresh signing certificate on demand, for free. To prevent impersonation, the developer proves their identity with an OIDC token: a cryptographically signed statement from a third party like Google, Microsoft, or GitHub that attests to the email address, username, or potentially other claims about the developer’s identity. The verifier can check that the username is correct and the certificate chain links back to Sigstore Fulcio’s root certificate, proving that someone with access to that account created the signature. Keyless signing is particularly useful because it can be integrated into a developer’s existing workflow-based deployment pipeline. This is frequently called provenance attestation or trusted publishing 8 . GitHub and GitLab provide OIDC tokens to Actions and CI/CD workflows that attest to the build workflow, the repository, and the commit hash. A workflow can use this token to obtain a signing certificate from Sigstore, sign the built package, and upload the signed package to the package repository. Since the signing certificate includes the commit hash and workflow details, this cryptographically links the built binary artifact to its source code. Provenance attestation via Sigstore is supported by Python’s PyPI , the npm Registry , RubyGems repository , and Maven Central . While Sigstore attestations are not mandatory, there is already better adoption than RubyGems’ optional support for developer-managed signing keys. Verification code is skipped, unconfigured, or nonexistent Unfortunately, just because these signatures exist does not mean they are being verified by package managers. In the npm package manager, the repository signatures are not checked when running npm install . Checking the signatures requires running npm audit signatures , which uses Sigstore to validate the registry public keys and then validates the signatures of the installed packages. pnpm recently added the pnpm audit signatures command , but that implementation fetches the registry public keys from the potentially malicious registry rather than verifying with Sigstore, so an adversary could simply add their own key and signature. Bun and Yarn currently lack an equivalent audit signatures command. In the NuGet package manager, the default signatureValidationMode is accept , which installs invalidly signed packages. The user must set this to require and configure the list of trusted signers, such as with dotnet nuget trust source . These configurations (which include the repository public keys) can be securely distributed within a nuget.config configuration file, functioning as a lockfile that locks the trusted signers. Ruby’s Gem and Bundler, and Java’s Maven and Gradle, which all use repositories with developer signatures, do not verify signatures by default. They require the user to manually add developer public keys ( gem cert --add ) or list the allowed public keys that should be trusted. In Maven, one can use the third-party pgpverify-maven-plugin with pgp-keys-map.list to specify the trusted PGP fingerprints. Gradle offers dependency verification , which works similarly. Finally, several package managers seemingly lack any sort of verification code at all. Pip , uv , and Poetry do not currently have a way to verify identity-based attestations described in PEP740. cpanminus does not have a way to verify the integrity of the repository-signed CHECKSUMS file. It once did, but in response to a verification bypass vulnerability , this verification code was removed . Even though PowerShell is supported on non-Windows platforms, Authenticode signature verification is not 9 . At one point, the PowerShell repository noted that this issue “should be fixed in a future release.” Go package management and transparency logs Go’s built-in package manager is the only one I tested that verifies signatures by default, and it also introduces one final concept for cryptographic package integrity. When go get or go mod download fetches a package 10 , it hashes the package contents and compares the hash, package name, and version against the checksum database . The contents of the database are registry-signed (analogous to PGP signatures in Perl’s PAUSE server), and the default checksum database public key is hardcoded in Go’s source code. As long as the checksum database’s private key is used honestly, this design ensures that the package name and version are enough to uniquely identify the binary contents of a package. As a result, the go.mod lockfile achieves package integrity without needing to store cryptographic hashes. 11 Go’s checksum database is an example of a transparency log, or an immutable, global, tamper-resistant log of metadata. The same capability is provided by Sigstore’s Rekor and certificate transparency logs. In package managers, it cryptographically ensures that the package manager only ever installs the same binaries recorded by the transparency log. If everyone agrees on the transparency log, then everyone agrees on the package contents. This makes it more difficult for an adversary to selectively and undetectably target a victim with a malicious package. Transparency logs can still fail if there are other vulnerabilities , the log’s private key is compromised, or no one checks the transparency log for malicious behavior. Of all the package managers I tested, Go performed the best at maintaining cryptographic integrity in the face of a compromised package repository or proxy. However, the registry-signature-like design means that much of the system’s trust is concentrated in a single private key. A proposed cryptographic design for package managers One potential approach that combines the ideas in this post is to include signature information in the lockfile. Rather than commit to the hash of a particular package, the lockfile could commit to a developer’s identity or public key. This reuses much of the infrastructure in place for lockfile hashes, but it separates the question of immediate updates from the question of package integrity. With this design, the lockfile could specify a single dependency version (for build reproducibility) or a lower bound (for immediate updates), and the included identity ensures that a malicious repository or proxy cannot easily tamper with whatever package version the manager resolves to. In addition, a transparency log can protect against selective targeting, building on Sigstore’s identity-based signing and transparency log service. Sigstore avoids long-lived keys by default, but it also supports self-managed keys, KMS providers, and hardware tokens. This gives an easily adopted and secure default while still giving flexibility to developers who desire more control over their keys. This idea is not new and not my own. Attestation identities are part of the pylock.toml Python lockfile specification , the trusted-keys in Gradle’s verification metadata , and the pgp-keys-map.list file in the pgpverify-maven-plugin for Maven. This is the direction that many package managers are already moving towards, as evidenced by the increasing adoption of Sigstore into publishing workflows, attention on supply-chain security, and bugfixes that specifically cite potential tampering by a malicious adversary. There is increasing recognition that this is a problem, and increasing appetite to fix it. It won’t be easy. There are many subtle nuances that have to be considered and addressed, signing verification code needs to be developed and audited, and developers need to adopt the resulting design. In many of the package managers I reviewed as part of this project, I found communities of people who have been thinking about and pushing for cryptographic integrity and package signing for years. They know best what those package managers need, and they deserve the resources to make this a reality. One of the greatest cryptographic success stories in the past decade has been the nearly universal adoption of HTTPS, driven in part by industry and community recognition of the security risks of unencrypted traffic, and the nonprofit Let’s Encrypt providing free and easy-to-use TLS certificates as a public good. Package signing is in a similar state now to where HTTPS was a decade ago: persistent adversaries are a huge concern, and cryptographic security is nearly nonexistent. Universal package signing is not here yet, but it is on the horizon. With the right attention and investment, we can make it a reality. Acknowledgments Thank you to William Woodruff for valuable discussions about lockfiles, identity signing, and the challenges of package manager security. This post focuses on dependency managers for source code rather than system package managers like APT, Chocolatey, or Homebrew. The line between the two is blurred, but concentrating on one helps highlight particular usage and deployment patterns in that group. ↩︎ Trail of Bits has several ongoing and completed projects to improve supply-chain security in some of these package ecosystems, including helping address both account takeover threats and the cryptographic integrity problem. ↩︎ cpanminus is included in the default Docker container for Perl , but the container build scripts patch cpanminus to use HTTPS by default. ↩︎ A subtle distinction here is that vcpkg must be updated using git pull in order to fetch the latest package hashes, shifting the question from securely installing packages to securely updating the package manager. For consistency with other package managers, we do not consider this question, and we note this as a limitation of our threat model. ↩︎ Gradle can have a verification-metadata.xml file with content hashes, even though gradle.lockfile does not. ↩︎ Note that some flutter subcommands, including flutter run and flutter test , call flutter pub get by default, so these commands can also overwrite the pubspec.lock file unless called with --no-pub . ↩︎ The SwiftPM client has two main ways to download packages: via Git and via the custom Swift Package Registry Service Specification. The latter supports signatures, and the server protocol is implemented by private services such as JFrog Artifactory and AWS CodeArtifact . As far as I can find, there is no repository for the general public that implements this protocol, so I tested the signatureless Git format. ↩︎ Trusted publishing can also refer to using OIDC tokens to authenticate to a package repository, and it does not necessarily involve identity-based signing. ↩︎ Although I did not test PowerShell on Windows, the documented default ExecutionPolicy behavior is to block scripts on Windows client machines, and to require a valid signature for Windows servers. This achieves package integrity. ↩︎ Go calls these downloadable artifacts “modules,” which consist of “packages.” For the sake of consistent terminology with the rest of the post, I use “package” in the general sense, not the Go-specific one. ↩︎ The go.sum file stores hashes, but it is not a lockfile . Instead, it is a local cache for entries from the checksum database. ↩︎

detail.abstract_excerpt: I tested 25 of the most popular package managers to check whether they detect a compromised package repository injecting malicious code into legitimate packages. This code integrity problem could be solved using cryptographic hashes or signatures, but many package managers are still vulnerable to this threat. Of the 25 package managers reviewed 1 , fewer than half used lockfiles that checked for tampering by default, and only two verified the integrity of every package they downloaded. Supply-chain attacks caused by developer compromise are a common story, but imagine what happens if ongoing mitigation attempts, including work by Trail of Bits 2 , are successful. If developers of popular packages are no longer the easiest targets, attackers will shift their focus to the next weakest link in the system: the package repositories that serve the code. The cryptographic answers to this problem are more subtle than they appear, and many implementations fall short due to deliberate design choices, resource prioritization, or the complexity of developer-friendly solutions. One natural answer is to include a cryptographic hash of a package’s contents in a lockfile and compare hashes after downloading the package. This automatic verification was the default behavior in about half of the package managers I tested, but others required extra configuration to include or verify these hashes, used hashes in a cryptographically insecure way, or lacked hashes entirely. This is summarized in the following table. Verifies integrity Go, vcpkg Verifies if lockfile is present Bun, Bundler, Cargo, npm, pnpm, Poetry, SwiftPM, uv, Yarn Verifies with lockfile + extra steps Conda, Gradle, Pip, NuGet, Pub Does not verify with lockfile or N/A CocoaPods, Composer, Conan, cpanminus, Gem, Maven, PowerShellGet, PSResourceGet, R Table 1: Lockfile-based security of a package manager fetching dependencies from a malicious repository, categorized by how much work it takes a developer to achieve integrity. Experimentally verified for a particular configuration. Caveats detailed below. Another natural approach is to use signatures, avoiding the need to securely distribute a hash for every package. However, in my tests, only Go verified signatures by default; others required extra configuration, lacked verification code, or did not support signatures. Verifies signatures Go Verifies with configuration Bundler, Gem, Gradle, Maven, npm, NuGet Missing or incomplete verification Bun, cpanminus, Pip, pnpm, Poetry, PowerShellGet, PSResourceGet, uv, Yarn No signatures available for verification Cargo, CocoaPods, Composer, Conan, Conda, Pub, R, SwiftPM, vcpkg Table 2: Signature-based security of various package managers. Also experimentally verified and subject to similar caveats. As both tables show, I found a surprising variation in the cryptographic designs and the level of protection they provide. Despite the challenges, I also found several communities on the frontier of this integrity problem that are bringing improved designs to reality. This post explores those variations, showing where certain designs fall short, why code integrity is harder to solve than it appears, and what cryptographic designs might be adopted in the future. Simulating malicious package repositories Studying the cryptographic behavior of 25 package managers is quite the challenge. I wanted to minimize manual analysis, but also be 100% confident when I claim an attack from a malicious package repository is possible. To solve this problem, I built a testing harness based on Docker containers and mitmproxy that dynamically evaluates the security of package managers against a malicious server. Figure 1: Experimental design of the test harness used to simulate malicious package repositories The Ubuntu-based Docker images include a package manager, sample code, and optionally a lockfile. There are conflicting opinions about whether to include lockfiles in source code repositories, so I tested both configurations. The harness instructs the package manager to fetch dependencies from the repository, and the resulting network request routes through a WireGuard network to a custom mitmproxy addon. Because the mitmproxy TLS CA is installed in the Docker image, the addon can fully manipulate the plaintext from the package repository, simulating a compromised server. I assumed any web-facing server could be compromised (e.g., Composer fetches metadata from Packagist and packages from GitHub), but backend resources, like any private signing keys, remain secure. The simulated repository embeds malicious code into the downloaded packages, and if the sample code executes the malware, the attack is successful. I tried to keep the experimental setup reflective of real-world usage, but there are limitations. I installed the latest package manager versions, followed quickstart guides for setting up sample projects inside the container, and picked popular packages from public repositories to infect. I ran package manager commands with default flags to see if extra steps, like modifying the project manifest or running extra commands, were needed to enforce cryptographic integrity. However, I am limited to testing a single package with a single package manager version on a single platform, and the test conditions (e.g., PowerShell and CocoaPods on Ubuntu) may not represent the most common usage patterns. The setup isn’t meant to show that every developer is vulnerable to a malicious package repository, just that a developer following reasonable conventions is. With the package managers installed and network intercept functional, one (mostly) promising observation is clear. HTTPS is (almost) everywhere Our harness architecture captures all network traffic, so it’s easy to test that package managers are using TLS and validating the certificates. In almost every package manager, they are. The exception is cpanminus, the frequently recommended package manager for Perl. cpanminus uses unencrypted HTTP by default to connect to the Perl package repository, allowing any active network attacker to inject malicious code into downloaded packages. This vulnerability has been known for years, but the cpanminus developer has not switched to HTTPS, since doing so would be a breaking change to default behavior. 3 Hash functions don’t always provide integrity By using the mitmproxy addon to modify the package repository responses, I could investigate how different package managers use cryptographic hashes. Hashes are a natural way to ensure that a downloaded file has not been tampered with, but the main question is how the package manager learns the correct hash in the first place. Microsoft’s vcpkg package manager for C and C++ libraries offers an interesting example. The package manager source code includes content hashes for thousands of dependencies. When a developer updates their library and wants to register the new content in vcpkg, they recompute the hash of their package and open a pull request against the vcpkg source code with the new hash and link to the package. When a package is downloaded by vcpkg, the hash is checked. So as long as the package manager is trusted, this approach is fully secure against a malicious package repository. 4 Hashes in lockfiles It is significantly more common that the package manager learns the correct hash via a lockfile. A lockfile is frequently created by a package manager, resides alongside a project’s source code, and references specific versions of dependencies needed by the project. If a developer checks a lockfile with cryptographic hashes into the source code repository, and the user’s package manager validates downloaded packages against the hashes, then the user’s dependencies perfectly match the developer’s. This is how it works for the Bun package manager for JavaScript projects. Installing a package with bun add updates the bun.lock lockfile; committing the lockfile to Git and calling bun install on another copy of the repo verifies the hash in the lockfile against the new copy of the dependency. Similar behavior is found in npm, pnpm, and Yarn (also JavaScript package managers); uv and Poetry (Python package managers); Bundler (for Ruby); Cargo (for Rust); and SwiftPM (for Swift). Other package managers support lockfiles, but with more steps than the standard add/restore process. Python’s Pip has experimental support for the pylock.toml format, and Conda has the optional library Conda lock . NuGet, the .NET package manager, generates a lockfile after adding the RestorePackagesWithLockFile property to the project. Many package managers (Maven, R, PowerShellGet, PSResourceGet, and cpanminus) do not have dedicated lockfiles, and some have lockfiles (Gradle’s gradle.lockfile 5 and Gem’s Gemfile.lock ) without hashes in them. Hashes present, but not for integrity Surprisingly, I found a few examples where the lockfiles had a hash, but could still be compromised by a malicious server. If there is a mismatch, Pub detects the error, but installs the package anyway. The existing content-hash from pubspec.lock doesn't match contents for: * uuid-4.6.0 from "https://pub.dev" This indicates one of: * The content has changed on the server since you created the pubspec.lock. * The pubspec.lock has been corrupted. The CocoaPods dependency manager for Swift and Objective-C has a similar pattern. Here is part of a Podfile.lock file for a project that uses the popular Files dependency. SPEC CHECKSUMS : Files : d88e31b84d65e754935053b1c584ea8e2320698a This 160-bit checksum is the SHA-1 hash of the Files Podspec , which contains the following link to the source code. The recent change to pnpm’s --frozen-lockfile is one example. Another example of this tension is the question of whether the lockfile should be committed to version control. Most modern guidance recommends committing the lockfile for applications, since the final build environment is fully controlled. The question is more complicated for libraries, since package managers often ignore libraries’ lockfiles to avoid locking to conflicting transitive dependencies. Committing the lockfile makes it easier to develop the library by sharing a consistent build environment with other developers, but excluding the lockfile makes it easier to catch conflicts with different dependency versions before they are found by users. Many package managers recommend committing the lockfile for libraries (e.g., npm , pnpm , Poetry , uv , and Yarn ), some recommend excluding it (e.g., Bundler ), and some leave it up to the developer (e.g., Cargo ). Many of these questions are explored in a recent study by Gamage et al. The authors explore lockfile design decisions for seven package managers, analyze published projects, and perform semi-structured interviews with 15 developers. They find that the practice of committing a lockfile varies by which package manager is used, and categorize five benefits to using lockfiles, as perceived by the interview subjects: build determinism, integrity, transparency into indirect dependencies, debugging, and security scanning. Some of the developers also preferred to not use lockfiles, citing a preference for end users to resolve to the latest version of a dependency, which may have more bug fixes and vulnerability patches. The diversity of package manager designs and views surrounding the purpose of lockfiles makes it difficult to prescribe a single recommendation. With regard to supply-chain integrity, it is common, but not universal, to view lockfiles as a source of integrity that should be committed with the source code. For package managers with lockfiles that do not provide cryptographic integrity, it is worth considering whether their users share that expectation. Even when lockfile hashes can provide cryptographic integrity, locking to specific package hashes means that users do not immediately receive subsequent updates or security fixes, since the newer package has a different hash. This leads to frequent lockfile bumping to distribute the latest hashes. Wanting immediate updates is a separate concern from wanting package integrity, but the current, common approach of using hashes in lockfiles is at odds with that goal. In conclusion, lockfile hashes are often, but not always, effective at providing cryptographic integrity, but do not work in every situation. Signatures are common; verification is not Signatures are a natural way to address these shortcomings, but implementations frequently fall short. In theory, developers could sign every release with their own private key, and the package manager could check the signature of the package it downloads from the package repository. In fact, signatures are relatively common in different package ecosystems, but proper signature validation is surprisingly lacking. The reality of using signatures to provide code integrity is more nuanced than it seems, and package managers have different approaches to the problem. Many package managers have no signatures available. Arguably, vcpkg does not need them, because all package hashes are distributed with the manager, but this leaves Cargo, CocoaPods, Composer, Conan, Conda, Pub, R, and SwiftPM 7 . The Conan developers are aware and previously decided not to fix it, citing several implementation challenges and suggesting organizations where integrity is critical could run their own repository server. Cargo developers are actively considering different signing designs, but this effort is still in progress. Composer developers have been implementing many new protections against supply-chain attacks, with future plans for artifact integrity. Repository signing One straightforward approach, known as repository signing, is when the package repository signs every package once it’s uploaded, and the repository’s public key is distributed with the package manager. This doesn’t solve the problem of a totally compromised package repository, since a malicious package repository could legitimately sign a malicious package, but it would protect against untrusted mirrors or a partial compromise of a package repository’s serving infrastructure. Repository signatures are used by the npm Registry , the NuGet Registry , and the PAUSE server for Perl module distribution. In the npm Registry, signatures are distributed within package metadata with repository-specific public keys . NuGet Registry repository signatures are found in .signature.p7s files within the distributed ZIP package, again with repository-specific public keys . The PAUSE server takes a different approach, using its GPG key to batch sign the cryptographic hashes of several packages at a time. Developer signing Developer signing involves the developer maintaining the private key and signing the package before uploading it to the repository for distribution. This prevents the package repository from tampering with the contents, but it also provides a way for the package repository to authenticate the uploader. There are two common approaches for a developer asserting their public key. In the first approach, the public key is distributed out-of-band. The Maven Central repository (used by Maven and Gradle) and the RubyGems repository (used by the gem and Bundler package managers) both support this type of developer signing. Maven Central uses PGP signatures, and developer keys are distributed by public keyservers . RubyGems uses self-signed certificates, and their distribution is left to the developers (e.g., rspec ). The major difference is that developer signing is mandatory for Maven Central, and optional for RubyGems. Developer signing is rare for RubyGems, due to the lack of an established chain of trust, and a previous attempt to introduce a certificate authority failed . The second approach involves a chain of trust. The NuGet Registry and PowerShell Gallery both support developer signatures. Neither makes signatures mandatory, but the PowerShell Gallery recommends it and the NuGet Registry has strict requirements if developer signing is used. In both, the developer’s key must chain to a trusted CA , and acquiring a valid code-signing certificate can cost hundreds of dollars per year. The benefit of this approach is that trusted root certificates can be preinstalled on the platform, allowing package managers to verify public keys. One downside of developer signing is that developers are responsible for key management, and they can lose the ability to update their code if they lose access to their key. Identity-based signing An increasingly common middle ground is “identity-based” or “keyless” signing from Sigstore . Rather than require developers to manage long-term private keys, a developer can use Sigstore’s Fulcio CA to issue a fresh signing certificate on demand, for free. To prevent impersonation, the developer proves their identity with an OIDC token: a cryptographically signed statement from a third party like Google, Microsoft, or GitHub that attests to the email address, username, or potentially other claims about the developer’s identity. The verifier can check that the username is correct and the certificate chain links back to Sigstore Fulcio’s root certificate, proving that someone with access to that account created the signature. Keyless signing is particularly useful because it can be integrated into a developer’s existing workflow-based deployment pipeline. This is frequently called provenance attestation or trusted publishing 8 . GitHub and GitLab provide OIDC tokens to Actions and CI/CD workflows that attest to the build workflow, the repository, and the commit hash. A workflow can use this token to obtain a signing certificate from Sigstore, sign the built package, and upload the signed package to the package repository. Since the signing certificate includes the commit hash and workflow details, this cryptographically links the built binary artifact to its source code. Provenance attestation via Sigstore is supported by Python’s PyPI , the npm Registry , RubyGems repository , and Maven Central . While Sigstore attestations are not mandatory, there is already better adoption than RubyGems’ optional support for developer-managed signing keys. Verification code is skipped, unconfigured, or nonexistent Unfortunately, just because these signatures exist does not mean they are being verified by package managers. In the npm package manager, the repository signatures are not checked when running npm install . Checking the signatures requires running npm audit signatures , which uses Sigstore to validate the registry public keys and then validates the signatures of the installed packages. pnpm recently added the pnpm audit signatures command , but that implementation fetches the registry public keys from the potentially malicious registry rather than verifying with Sigstore, so an adversary could simply add their own key and signature. Bun and Yarn currently lack an equivalent audit signatures command. In the NuGet package manager, the default signatureValidationMode is accept , which installs invalidly signed packages. The user must set this to require and configure the list of trusted signers, such as with dotnet nuget trust source . These configurations (which include the repository public keys) can be securely distributed within a nuget.config configuration file, functioning as a lockfile that locks the trusted signers. Ruby’s Gem and Bundler, and Java’s Maven and Gradle, which all use repositories with developer signatures, do not verify signatures by default. They require the user to manually add developer public keys ( gem cert --add ) or list the allowed public keys that should be trusted. In Maven, one can use the third-party pgpverify-maven-plugin with pgp-keys-map.list to specify the trusted PGP fingerprints. Gradle offers dependency verification , which works similarly. Finally, several package managers seemingly lack any sort of verification code at all. Pip , uv , and Poetry do not currently have a way to verify identity-based attestations described in PEP740. cpanminus does not have a way to verify the integrity of the repository-signed CHECKSUMS file. It once did, but in response to a verification bypass vulnerability , this verification code was removed . Even though PowerShell is supported on non-Windows platforms, Authenticode signature verification is not 9 . At one point, the PowerShell repository noted that this issue “should be fixed in a future release.” Go package management and transparency logs Go’s built-in package manager is the only one I tested that verifies signatures by default, and it also introduces one final concept for cryptographic package integrity. When go get or go mod download fetches a package 10 , it hashes the package contents and compares the hash, package name, and version against the checksum database . The contents of the database are registry-signed (analogous to PGP signatures in Perl’s PAUSE server), and the default checksum database public key is hardcoded in Go’s source code. As long as the checksum database’s private key is used honestly, this design ensures that the package name and version are enough to uniquely identify the binary contents of a package. As a result, the go.mod lockfile achieves package integrity without needing to store cryptographic hashes. 11 Go’s checksum database is an example of a transparency log, or an immutable, global, tamper-resistant log of metadata. The same capability is provided by Sigstore’s Rekor and certificate transparency logs. In package managers, it cryptographically ensures that the package manager only ever installs the same binaries recorded by the transparency log. If everyone agrees on the transparency log, then everyone agrees on the package contents. This makes it more difficult for an adversary to selectively and undetectably target a victim with a malicious package. Transparency logs can still fail if there are other vulnerabilities , the log’s private key is compromised, or no one checks the transparency log for malicious behavior. Of all the package managers I tested, Go performed the best at maintaining cryptographic integrity in the face of a compromised package repository or proxy. However, the registry-signature-like design means that much of the system’s trust is concentrated in a single private key. A proposed cryptographic design for package managers One potential approach that combines the ideas in this post is to include signature information in the lockfile. Rather than commit to the hash of a particular package, the lockfile could commit to a developer’s identity or public key. This reuses much of the infrastructure in place for lockfile hashes, but it separates the question of immediate updates from the question of package integrity. With this design, the lockfile could specify a single dependency version (for build reproducibility) or a lower bound (for immediate updates), and the included identity ensures that a malicious repository or proxy cannot easily tamper with whatever package version the manager resolves to. In addition, a transparency log can protect against selective targeting, building on Sigstore’s identity-based signing and transparency log service. Sigstore avoids long-lived keys by default, but it also supports self-managed keys, KMS providers, and hardware tokens. This gives an easily adopted and secure default while still giving flexibility to developers who desire more control over their keys. This idea is not new and not my own. Attestation identities are part of the pylock.toml Python lockfile specification , the trusted-keys in Gradle’s verification metadata , and the pgp-keys-map.list file in the pgpverify-maven-plugin for Maven. This is the direction that many package managers are already moving towards, as evidenced by the increasing adoption of Sigstore into publishing workflows, attention on supply-chain security, and bugfixes that specifically cite potential tampering by a malicious adversary. There is increasing recognition that this is a problem, and increasing appetite to fix it. It won’t be easy. There are many subtle nuances that have to be considered and addressed, signing verification code needs to be developed and audited, and developers need to adopt the resulting design. In many of the package managers I reviewed as part of this project, I found communities of people who have been thinking about and pushing for cryptographic integrity and package signing for years. They know best what those package managers need, and they deserve the resources to make this a reality. One of the greatest cryptographic success stories in the past decade has been the nearly universal adoption of HTTPS, driven in part by industry and community recognition of the security risks of unencrypted traffic, and the nonprofit Let’s Encrypt providing free and easy-to-use TLS certificates as a public good. Package signing is in a similar state now to where HTTPS was a decade ago: persistent adversaries are a huge concern, and cryptographic security is nearly nonexistent. Universal package signing is not here yet, but it is on the horizon. With the right attention and investment, we can make it a reality. Acknowledgments Thank you to William Woodruff for valuable discussions about lockfiles, identity signing, and the challenges of package manager security. This post focuses on dependency managers for source code rather than system package managers like APT, Chocolatey, or Homebrew. The line between the two is blurred, but concentrating on one helps highlight particular usage and deployment patterns in that group. ↩︎ Trail of Bits has several ongoing and completed projects to improve supply-chain security in some of these package ecosystems, including helping address both account takeover threats and the cryptographic integrity problem. ↩︎ cpanminus is included in the default Docker container for Perl , but the container build scripts patch cpanminus to use HTTPS by default. ↩︎ A subtle distinction here is that vcpkg must be updated using git pull in order to fetch the latest package hashes, shifting the question from securely installing packages to securely updating the package manager. For consistency with other package managers, we do not consider this question, and we note this as a limitation of our threat model. ↩︎ Gradle can have a verification-metadata.xml file with content hashes, even though gradle.lockfile does not. ↩︎ Note that some flutter subcommands, including flutter run and flutter test , call flutter pub get by default, so these commands can also overwrite the pubspec.lock file unless called with --no-pub . ↩︎ The SwiftPM client has two main ways to download packages: via Git and via the custom Swift Package Registry Service Specification. The latter supports signatures, and the server protocol is implemented by private services such as JFrog Artifactory and AWS CodeArtifact . As far as I can find, there is no repository for the general public that implements this protocol, so I tested the signatureless Git format. ↩︎ Trusted publishing can also refer to using OIDC tokens to authenticate to a package repository, and it does not necessarily involve identity-based signing. ↩︎ Although I did not test PowerShell on Windows, the documented default ExecutionPolicy behavior is to block scripts on Windows client machines, and to require a valid signature for Windows servers. This achieves package integrity. ↩︎ Go calls these downloadable artifacts “modules,” which consist of “packages.” For the sake of consistent terminology with the rest of the post, I use “package” in the general sense, not the Go-specific one. ↩︎ The go.sum file stores hashes, but it is not a lockfile . Instead, it is a local cache for entries from the checksum database. ↩︎

items.headline: Attacking UOV-based Signatures over divided power algebras. We introduce a family of divided power wedge attacks on UOV-type systems over finite fields of arbitrary characteristic.
items.summary: We introduce a family of divided power wedge attacks on UOV-type systems over finite fields of arbitrary characteristic. The construction extends the characteristic-two exterior-algebra construction of Merz and Ran to the $p$-truncated polynomial ring, where $p$ is the field characteristic. An attack level controls which divided-power relations are adjoined, balancing a lower solving degree against increased average Macaulay row weight.

items.headline: Affine Combiners for Reed-Solomon Proximity Gaps. Reed–Solomon proximity gaps establish soundness guarantees for protocols that test received words through random combinations.
items.summary: Reed–Solomon proximity gaps establish soundness guarantees for protocols that test received words through random combinations. For length-$n$ codes over $\mathbb{F}_q$, classical scalar combiners achieve error $O(n/q)$ in the unique-decoding regime, with larger known bounds near the Johnson radius. We prove smaller error bounds using affine combiners, which combine two received words $f,g$ as $f(x)+(\alpha+\beta x)g(x)$, where $\alpha,\beta$ are independent uniform elements of $\mathbb{F}_q$.

items.summary_tr: Reed-Solomon yakınlık boşlukları, alınan kelimeleri rastgele kombinasyonlar yoluyla test eden protokoller için sağlamlık garantileri oluşturur. $\mathbb{F}_q$ üzerindeki uzunluk-$n$ kodları için, klasik skaler birleştiriciler, Johnson yarıçapı yakınında bilinen daha büyük sınırlarla, benzersiz kod çözme rejiminde $O(n/q)$ hatasına ulaşır. detail.method_architecture: For length-$n$ codes over $\mathbb{F}_q$, classical scalar combiners achieve error $O(n/q)$ in the unique-decoding regime, with larger known bounds near the Johnson radius. detail.findings_tradeoffs: For output degree bound $d=\rho n$, fixed $\rho\in(0,1)$ and $0<\eta<1-\sqrt{\rho}$, and sufficiently large block length $n$, we prove mutual correlated agreement (MCA) with one coordinate of agreement loss at threshold $A=\lceil(\sqrt{\rho}+\eta)n\rceil$, with error $O_{\rho,\eta}\left(\frac{1}{q}+\frac{n^2}{q^2}\right)$. The result holds over arbitrary evaluation domains in every finite field, including prime and binary extension fields. The agreement threshold can approach the Johnson threshold, beyond unique decoding. For $q\ge n^2$, our error is $O_{\rho,\eta}(1/q)$, an asymptotic factor-$n$ separation from scalar combiners: we prove that their worst-case MCA error is $\Omega_{\rho,\eta}(n/q)$ at the same agreement threshold and with the same one-coordinate loss. We also prove that affine combiners incur worst-case error $\Omega_{\rho,\eta}(n/q)$ when no agreement loss is allowed. Thus one coordinate of agreement loss is necessary for our guarantee; this relaxation of standard MCA reduces the guaranteed common agreement fraction by at most $1/n$. We also extend the result to $k$-variate Reed–Muller codes on subfield grids, obtaining MCA error $O_{\rho,\eta,k}(q^{-k})$ for fixed $\rho,\eta,k$, sufficiently large $n$, and $q\ge n^{k+1}$, with agreement loss $n^{1-1/k}$.

items.headline: ECLIPSE: Strongly Unforgeable Isogeny Signatures from the Prime-Degree Variant of PRISM
items.summary: ECLIPSE is the prime-degree signature construction the PRISM authors describe beside their salted scheme, with that salt, implemented. It exists because a two-dimensional isogeny signature carries an auxiliary isogeny the hash does not bind: the SQIsign round-3 specification says SQIsign cannot be strongly unforgeable for that reason, and PRISM's prime-degree variant has no auxiliary isogeny but was published without parameters, code or a running verifier. This paper is the first implementation, on the SQIsign round-3 primes: a verifier that evaluates the paper's criterion through one isogeny chain and a pull-back, a canonical wire format whose strict decoder recovers one coefficient from two Weil pairings, randomisable keys, two independent implementations that accept each other's signatures, and one key in both roles: a MIKE key pair at the level I prime is an ECLIPSE key pair, the public curve re-encoded and the signing key derived from the MIKE secret alone, with MIKE's code untouched.

items.headline: On the Pitfalls of Modeling Individual Knowledge. The concept of knowledge has been central in cryptography, especially within cryptographic proof systems.
items.summary: The concept of knowledge has been central in cryptography, especially within cryptographic proof systems. Traditionally, research in this area considers an abstract \emph{prover} defending a claim that it knows a message $M$. Recently, a stronger concept—termed ``individual'' (Dziembowski et al., CRYPTO'23) or ``complete'' (Kelkar et al., CCS'24) knowledge—has emerged.

As we argue in the paper, this concept also appears in earlier work on ``non-outsourceable puzzles'' (Miller et al., CCS'15), which implicitly assumes that performing quickly complex computation on a string $M$ implies storing it on a single machine. In this line of work, the authors typically rely on the algorithms whose computation requires a massive number of queries to a hash function $H$. In the full version of this paper, we will provide their formal security analysis in the individual cryptography model of Dziembowski et al. (CRYPTO'23).
